The radar cross section (RCS) of an object is a crucial parameter in a wide range of applications, including military and civilian applications.
Reverberation chambers (RCs) have become a promising alternative testing facility for various electromagnetic applications, including RCS measurement.

The method used in this paper involves a two-step process: first, the reflection coefficient of an antenna oriented towards the target is measured; second, the same measurement is performed without the target.
The distance R between the antenna and target was chosen to be greater than 2D^2/λ, where D is the largest dimension of the target and λ is the minimum considered wavelength.
The amplitude of the forward and backward traveling waves between the antenna and target is estimated using the Friis equation.
The phase variation is assumed to be constant along the target and corresponds to the wave propagation at the speed of light c along the forward and backward paths of two times the distance R.
The measurements were performed in the 9.75 GHz to 10.25 GHz frequency range, with the antenna and target separated by a distance of 2.95 m.
The Lowest Useable Frequency (LUF) of the reverberation chamber is around 200 MHz.

The RCS pattern obtained in the reverberation chamber for the same stirrer position as the reference measurement showed good agreement with the anechoic chamber results, except for the lowest levels of RCS.
The mean relative error between the RCS patterns obtained with a stirrer position shift remains low (below 20%) for shifts up to 20 degrees, but becomes extremely high for a shift of 36 degrees.
The authors suggest that the same stirrer position should be chosen for the two measurements (with and without the target) to increase the RCS pattern estimation accuracy.

The reverberation chamber can be a valid and economically convenient alternative to the anechoic chamber for RCS measurements of canonical targets, but care must be taken to ensure the same stirrer position is used for both measurements.
The impact of the stirrer position shift on the RCS estimation accuracy depends on the geometry of the stirrer itself.
